items.title: 4.7.2 Maximum amount of product and amount of any unreacted excess reagent

blocks.title: Excess reagent
blocks.text: The reactants present in larger amounts than the stoichiometry of the reaction needs, which remain unreacted at the end of the reaction, are the excess reagents (excess or non-limiting reactants).

Consider 2H2(g) + O2(g) gives 2H2O(l). When 2 moles of hydrogen (4 g) react with 2 moles of oxygen (64 g), only 2 moles (36 g) of water form, because 2 moles of hydrogen need only 1 mole (32 g) of oxygen; hydrogen is the limiting reactant and 1 mole of oxygen is left. When 1 mole of O2 and 1 mole of H2 are mixed, all the hydrogen reacts and oxygen is left over, because 1 mole of H2 needs only half a mole of O2; the remaining half mole is excess.
Sample Problem 4.19: 30 g of CH4 with 50 g of O2

Methane burns as CH4 + 2O2 gives CO2 + 2H2O. Step 1, write the balanced equation. Step 2, moles of each reactant: CH4 = 30 / 16 = 1.875 mol; O2 = 50 / 32 = 1.563 mol. Step 3, product from each: 1 mol CH4 gives 1 mol CO2, so 1.875 mol CO2; 2 mol O2 give 1 mol CO2, so 1.563 x 0.5 = 0.7815 mol CO2. Oxygen gives less, so O2 is the limiting reactant. Step 4, mass of product: 0.7815 x 44 = 34.39 g of CO2. Step 5, the limiting reactant fixes how much excess reactant is used: 2 mol O2 react with 1 mol CH4, so 1.563 mol O2 use 1.563 x 1/2 = 0.7815 mol CH4. Step 6, excess left = taken - used = 1.875 - 0.7815 = 1.0935 mol CH4, which is 1.0935 x 16.0 = 17.5 g of methane unreacted.

blocks.alt: Left: bars for the moles of CH4 and O2 available, then bars for the CO2 each could make, the shorter oxygen bar marked as limiting, with the product mass and the leftover methane written below. Right: a box on the hydrogen and oxygen example and a box with the percentage yield formula and its reasons.
blocks.caption: Finding the limiting reactant, the maximum product, the excess left over and the percentage yield (original diagram after Sample Problem 4.19).
blocks.long_description: Thirty grams of methane is 1.875 mol and fifty grams of oxygen 1.563 mol. Methane could make 1.875 mol of CO2 but oxygen only 0.7815 mol, so oxygen limits and 34.39 g of CO2 is the most that can form. The oxygen uses 0.7815 mol of methane, leaving 1.0935 mol, 17.5 g, unreacted. In the hydrogen example 2 mol of H2 with 2 mol of O2 give only 36 g of water and leave 1 mol of oxygen. The percentage yield compares the actual product with this theoretical maximum.

blocks.prompt: 34.0 g of ammonia reacts with 80.0 g of oxygen by 4NH3 + 5O2 = 4NO + 6H2O. Find the limiting reactant, the maximum mass of NO, and the excess reactant left (H = 1.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0).
blocks.explanation: NH3: 34.0 / 17.0 = 2.0 mol; O2: 80.0 / 32.0 = 2.5 mol. NO from NH3: 2.0 mol (4 : 4); NO from O2: 2.5 x 4/5 = 2.0 mol. Both give the same, so the mixture is in exact ratio and neither is in excess; the maximum NO is 2.0 mol x 30.0 g/mol = 60.0 g and no reactant is left over.

items: Excess reagent: the reactant left unreacted. Product from the limiting reactant is the maximum; excess used = limiting moles x ratio; excess left = taken - used.
30 g CH4 + 50 g O2: O2 limits (0.7815 mol CO2, 34.39 g); 0.7815 mol CH4 used, 1.0935 mol = 17.5 g left.
